utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. To the extent the transcript of yesterday, page 22918 may have caused any confusion as to whether the document marked for identification under number 534 would have been a P or a D document, it is a Defence document. Having said this -- yes, but I don't receive any -- I have no volume. Yes, now it's better. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Veljovic. Perhaps there is no need to remind you but I nevertheless do, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Weber will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday we left off discussing the topic of modified air bombs. At the end of the day, I asked you about Vladimir Radojcic and his awareness of modified air bombs. In your answer, on transcript page 22956, you stated: "He knows of one instance when it fell on his own positions but went unexploded." How do you know that Vladimir Radojcic knows of this one instance?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber kindly: I had two strokes, and I commanded units at different levels, from company and squad upwards. Could I please explain to the Court all of this a bit more extensively? Could I please be given the authority to do that? Because all these questions are geared towards air bombs and nothing else. Sir -- I mean, Mr. Prosecutor, I came here to defend General Mladic, and I provided a written statement for him as well which has been corroborated by this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will respond to the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stop. I would like to correct you. You did not come here to defend Mr. Mladic. You came here to give testimony to the truth. You're not either in favour or -- or against Mr. Mladic. That should be clear to you that you are not here in a position to defend. And I would invite you to just answer the questions Mr. Weber considers relevant. And I also would like to ask you to explain, perhaps in two more words, about the strokes you referred to. What did you want to say to us when you told us about the two strokes you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I told you that I survived these two strokes. I am a sick man, after all. I cannot remember each and every thing. Please take that into consideration. And what I said about air bombs being imprecise is the following: No artillery piece in the world is precise. Not rockets, not mortars that have been used for hundreds of years. The shell remains in the barrel, and these things that can happen. There are so many things that have to be taken into account; how the soldier feels, and then maybe the shell gets stuck in the barrel, and so on. Nothing is accidental. Perhaps there can be even a 3-kilometre deviation. The American ones were made according to the most up-to-date technology, and there was a mistake of a few seconds, and all this technology and all this money went to waste. So all use of artillery can turn into collateral damage, as the Americans call it. So I would like to explain that this air bomb, too, is imprecise. So that is why I thought that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. First of all, have you been criticised for what you said yesterday? Did anyone criticise you and say, "Well, this is not correct or accurate," or -- what you told yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes -- no. I'm just giving yes or no answers. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it's within my domain just to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Let me just -- could you please answer my question whether anyone criticised you for what you said yesterday, because if you don't remember things, and you talked about that, just tell us. But was there anyone who criticised you for your yesterday's testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody criticised me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nobody commented on it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Yes," meaning no one did; or, yes, someone did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody criticised me, nobody. I mean -- but this is going so fast, and they are cutting me off, and they are putting all these questions that I have this underlying stress --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that causes anxiety. And, say, five years ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I mean, we are not talking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'm going to stop you now. You should stop talking when I indicate to you that you're supposed to stop talking. Now just answer the questions. If you don't remember something, no problem, you tell us. Just stick to the facts. Do not elaborate on how imprecise American, Russian, Chinese, African weapons are. Just listen careful to the question, answer the question, and leave it to that. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, I'm just going to follow-up on a couple of matters that His Honour just asked you. Has anyone mentioned your testimony in any way at all to you since yesterday?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody. Except for what I mind, and what I mind is that you keep asking me things from the past, things that happened seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, again, we are talking about the past. Therefore, what questions will be put to you is for Mr. Weber to decide, and if there is any objection to that, the Defence will object. You should not intervene in the line of questioning. You just should focus on answering the questions. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, since yesterday, have you seen any media coverage or any information that might be publicly available related to the testimony you gave?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I haven't been following the media here. Just the football games.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to return to the question I asked you at the outset of today. Yesterday, at transcript page 22956, you stated that Mr. Radojcic knows of one instance when a modified air bomb fell on his own positions but went unexploded. How do you know that Vladimir Radojcic knows of this one instance?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know because I was operations officer in the corps and he told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did he tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did this one instance occur?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when, which month.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you approximate what time of year?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometime in the summer, May, June, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say it fell on his own positions, is it correct that you were referring to the positions of the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where in the Ilidza Brigade's zone of responsibility was this modified air bomb fired from?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They had urban positions and positions in a forested areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I just seek clarification. You said that you were told -- that Mr. Radojcic told you about it in 1995. And when asked about when this event had happened, you said it was May, June, perhaps in summer, you thought. Of that same year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When this modified air bomb fell on his own positions, where did it fall?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When was the last time that you spoke with Vladimir Radojcic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to him here when we were here in The Hague, before this break. But I didn't ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. How many days have you been in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today it's 14 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How many times have you seen Mr. Radojcic during these 14 days?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he went back home. And then I hear that he returned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. How many times did you see him before he went back home?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, say, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How did you hear that he returned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know from the lawyers and those officials from the Victims and Witness Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did the lawyers tell you that he returned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they said that to Milos, and they said before he was supposed to return that he would be coming back on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "Milos," is it correct that you're referring to Milos Skrba?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Last night around 9.00 he said that to me. He said that Vladimir came and that he's going home, and this morning we said goodbye.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that last night you spoke with Milos Skrba?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really talk. He talked to the lawyers around 8.00 or 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "the lawyers," are you referring to the lawyers of Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Stojanovic, I guess. As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And Mr. Skrba told you that he had spoken with Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I take it you're aware that Mr. Skrba is a witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Going back to my question, how many times did you speak with Mr. Radojcic before he went home?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you a few times; two, three, four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this in person? These two to three, four times.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what it is that you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you meet with him face to face?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I talked to him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How many times have you talked with Milos Skrba since you've been in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before he went out to testify on Monday, whenever, we talked often and took walks along the seashore.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could just have one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to return to your testimony about modified air bombs --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours had any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no further questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case, at transcript page 5910, you stated: "And in our areas inhabited by Serbs and in the area of responsibility of the Republika Srpska Army, there were no production facilities for air bombs. And I said that launchers were made just by ordinary craftsmen. This was not done in a factory. This was an imperfect weapon that caused great risk for the crew, for our own forces. It is a very inaccurate weapon because bombs have to be dropped from the planes. That's what they're made of. I think I have already explained all that." Do you stand by this testimony today?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just this: The factory --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- had to make certain machine parts --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to go through it step by step as I was doing yesterday. How did the modified air bombs cause great risk for the crew that was launching them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because it can explode nearby. It can fall nearby. It can also not reach its target, not go far away and then it can destroy them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the Karadzic case, at transcript page 29270, you were asked: "Q. And it's true, isn't it, that air bombs are actually highly destructive?" You answered: "Yes. From 250 to 500 kilogrammes, or even up to 1.000 kilogrammes, intending to be launched from aircraft. However, that civil war forced people to devise those launchers, but we were supposed to use those air bombs only in wilderness where there were no human settlements, where there was no habitation, and all they created was panic among the troops." Do you stand by this testimony today?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In this answer you said, "all they created was panic amongst the troops." Yesterday you also confirmed that modified air bombs fired in urban areas would have posed a risk of hitting civilians. Is it correct that modified air bombs would have created panic, if they were used in an urban area where civilians were present?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it has a lethal effect, more than one shell. Also it creates greater craters. Not like some people think, that it has a lethal effect only at 150 metres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- I'm going to show you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to show you an exhibit that you were shown in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter 18593.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say 185?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. 18593.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 10 August 1994 order for further operations from SRK Commander Dragomir Milosevic. As I said, you were previously shown this document in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have the last page of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention first to the initials SC, which appear to the left of General Milosevic's signature. Is it correct that these are the initials for Cedo Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do these initials, the first ones, the first ones listed before the slash, do these initials indicate that this is the individual who drafted this order for the approval of General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the left-hand side is the person who drafts the order, and then it is approved and signed by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, I'd like to direct your attention to the sentence immediately above item 6 on this order. It states: "2 air bomb launchers will be ready for firing at Mosevicko Brdo structure and 2 launchers for firing at Gradina, Konjsko Brdo and Velika Bukva." This document is from August 1994. Is it correct that the SRK had deployed and begun using modified air bomb launchers by this time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August 1994, I was not in the corps, and I am not aware of this. I see that Mosevicko Brdo and Konjsko Brdo, et cetera, I see that that is a wasteland on the Nisic plateau where bombs were thrown. All of these places here, it's all afforested. It is not accessible. It is only on foot that the army could have taken this. There are no villages there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 18593 receives number P6604, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6604 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to move on and discuss some other topics with you. A general question here: Is it correct that Milovan Bjelica is a relative of yours. His father and your mother are brother and sister; correct? My apologies for mispronouncing the name.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Milovan Bjelica is related to me, but it's not that we are related in the way you mentioned. My mother is from the brother, and he is from the sister. It's called first cousins, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mr. Bjelica was a member of the Sokolac SDS?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And president of the Executive Board of the party for Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I am now going to direct your attention to the time-period of April 1992. You discussed this time-period in paragraph 36 of your statement admitted as D532.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 11755.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before you is a published copy of an interview that your relative Milovan Bjelica gave to Srpsko Oslobodjenje on 27 December 1994. This article was previously shown to you during the Karadzic case, and I would like to discuss a few parts of it with you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of the English translation. It's still the same page on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in the B/C/S original, I'd like to direct your attention to the bottom of the third column from the left in the article. Do you see the question that asks: "How did you arm the people?"

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Toward the end of the answer to this question, Mr. Bjelica stated: "First we took the equipment and weapons from Western Herzegovina, from Gabela, which we brought to Romanija. Then we took the equipment from Central Bosnia, from Visoko, from Sarajevo municipalities which were not under our control. And our greatest success was taking the equipment and weapons from Faletici." Is it correct that the taking of weapons and equipment that Mr. Bjelica describes occurred in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it occurred in April 1992 while we were still the JNA. The 216th Brigade intervened on orders from the 4th Corps of the former JNA in order to assist the guards securing the JNA warehouses. The Muslim forces had broken into the warehouses and started taking away weapons. The 216th Brigade was asked to provide protection for the magazines -- for the warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, one second.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was between the 13th and the 14th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, let's continue on with this article. After the next question, Mr. Bjelica is asked: "It was probably Gagovic?" And he answers: "No, it was Simovic but Gagovic was there as well. We did it by night in April 1992. We entered with hundred trucks on the first night. There was a group of young men, activists of SDS, which I was leading, and also a group from Pale from the party led by Radomir Kojic, then unit of current Colonel Jovan Bartula, then Ilija Maletic with his people from Stari Grad. This depot contained all weapons of the Territorial Defence of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. We rated in there the first night, and as soon as we entered the depot, the Green Berets and special forces of Dragan Bikic started surrounding the barracks. We repelled the attack and started pulling out the weapons. The first night, we took the whole artillery and weapons. There was about three hundred artillery tubes, from thirty five to fifty thousand rifles as well as other equipment." Just for the sake of completeness here, before I go through some other things, a little further on in this answer, he says: "We were helped by the unit of Colonel Dragoljub Milosevic, i.e., the first Romanija Brigade." And then it also states: "And we brought all the weapons and equipment to the territory of Romanija in three days." Is it correct that between 600 and 700 soldiers of the 216th JNA Brigade participated in these operations?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. It was the 216th Brigade and not the 1st Romanija Infantry and not a JNA Brigade. As for the Bjelica, I didn't see him on the 14th or the 13th. I didn't see him anywhere. Nor did I see Kojic or Maletic. On the 13th or 14th we were there. Now, whether they had been there before, I don't know, but on those dates I didn't see them. There were not 50.000 rifles there, and it wasn't the warehouse of the entire BiH Territorial Defence. It was just a warehouse of the city of Sarajevo. It was between 25- and 30.000 rifles. As for the 300 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- cannons, well, the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina TO didn't have as many.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please listen to my questions, and we'll go very quickly today. Is it correct that the 216th Brigade took some of these weapons and placed them in Mokro in the barracks and some of the weapons went to the Territorial Defence of Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. We transferred parts of the weapons to Travno and to Sokolac. And the 216th Brigade had its own weapons and its own warehouses. The 216th Brigade didn't take any of the weapons from the warehouse. The barracks in Mokro belonged to the JNA. As for Sokolac, it was taken to a factory and the weapons were kept there, although I don't know what became of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This reference to Colonel Dragoljub Milosevic, is it correct that this is actually a reference to Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He commanded the 216th Mountain Brigade of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I do want to ask you about two other names in the passage. Is it correct that Radomir Kojic was a policeman at the beginning of the war and then he became the commander of the Trebevic Battalion of the 1st Romanija Brigade around the 31st of October 1992 when Milorad Lalovic died?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Milorad Lalovic but Lolovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Is the rest of what I said correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. He came after the 31st of October, because Milorad Lolovic was killed on that day. He came about a week later from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some police personnel withdrew as part of their battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, Radomir Kojic was a member of the 1st Romanija Brigade between the end of October 1992 and 7 August 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After the 7th of August, 1995, is it correct that Radomir Kojic was assigned to the 4th Slpbr after this brigade was formed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He became the Chief of Staff of the 4th Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade; in other words, my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: From the beginning of the war in 1992, Jovan Bartula was a commander of a mixed anti-armour regiment of the SRK; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 11755 into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 11755 receives number P6605, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6605 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case, at transcript page 5710, you were asked a series of questions and answers: "Q. What happened with regular soldiers after the time you mentioned?" Your answer: "Ordinary soldiers of other ethnicities put down their weapons and went home." "Q. What did you do? "A. I remained with my unit. "Q. What time specifically are you talking about?" Your answer: "I'm talking about April and May 1992." Do you stand by this testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to move to another topic here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if the witness testified in a previous case ability other ethnicities, wouldn't it be good --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to know what the ethnicity is as he started thinking from?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, when you stated that ordinary soldiers of other ethnicities put down their weapons, is it correct that these soldiers were Croat and Muslim?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some officers were Croats, but there were no Croats in the area of Sokolac, Rogatica, and Vlasenica -- or perhaps just a few. For the most part, they were Muslims, and they were the most numerous group in the 216th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was about ordinary soldiers, not about officers. When you said "ordinary soldiers of other ethnicities, did you mean to say other than Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that Bascarsija was the most culturally and historically important part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Bascarsija is the old part of Sarajevo and it is comprised of small houses and buildings; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Old houses built in the Turkish style. The Ottoman empire reigned in that part of the world leaving its culture traces behind as well as the Austrian Hungarian Empire. Such buildings were not to be targeted a General Milosevic personally ordered. Even if fire was opened from such buildings, we were ordered not to engage them. We only used one Howitzer, 150 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Had we fired from a single Howitzer battery --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- all of Bascarsija would have been gone. And you could actually check that. It is the same as it had been in 1991. It was preserved, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to be clear on your view here. Is it correct that you view that it would be inappropriate for the SRK to target Bascarsija because of the culture importance of its buildings and the significant presence of civilians?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Veljovic, there were SRK orders and fire plans to target Bascarsija; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such orders. Actually, the order was not to fire at Bascarsija unless ordered by the commander. I didn't see any other documents to that effect. So fire could only be opened on -- if personally proved by General Milosevic while he was in command, and I presume the same was in place during Galic's commanding. And you can check. Bascarsija remains the same as it had been before the war. The houses there are so old and derelict that they are so soft that a single shell could cause major damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please listen to my questions. There is no need to repeat your answers. It's clear what you said so far. Is it correct, then, that any time the SRK filed a shell on Bascarsija it was approved by the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No shell was ever fired at Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through some stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P4423.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, before you is a 26 November 1992 SRK order from Radislav Cvetkovic to the 4th MAP and 4th MPOAP. Is it correct that these two regiments were controlled at the corps level?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that they were controlled by the corps command. At the time, I wasn't with the command of the corps, since this dates back to the 26th of November. It was received by the artillery chief and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the artillery commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to go through the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have the last page of the order in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to again direct your attention to the initials over to the left, and we see the initials RC. Is it correct that this would mean that Radislav Cvetkovic was the drafter of this document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely. And the chief of artillery also signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to page 2 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under the section of this order entitled: "Firing Tasks," Colonel Cvetkovic orders the engagement of fire on a number of locations. I'd like to direct your attention to the third paragraph from the top of this page in the B/C/S original. This is the second paragraph from the top in the English translation. The order states: "Support the offensive by engaging fire along the following axis," the last of which is Borija-Bascarsija. Is it correct that this order indicates that fire should be engaged from Borija, which is in the SRK territory, and into Bascarsija? That is the axis that this order indicates should be fired upon.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I believe under item (c), the third paragraph from the top of the page. It's about the first -- a third of the page down.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "open fire in order to support." And the routes are Ciglana, Kobjeglava, Pitslik [phoen], Cuprija. Basic sector --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you, Witness. I think you're reading from the wrong paragraph. If you would look at the top of the page, it starts with a C, where it reads "vatreni zadaci." And then the second and the third paragraph start with the same word, "Podrzati." Now, Mr. Weber wants you to focus on the third paragraph; that is a two-line paragraph in your language. You see that? It refers to giving support on certain axes, the first one Faletici-Zmajevac; and second one Mrkovici-Breka; and the third one, and that's what Mr. Weber is focusing at, Borija-Bascarsija. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's correct that this order indicates that fire should be engaged from Borija and into Bascarsija; correct? Along that axis.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would need to ask that the gentleman who drafted this order. At the time, I was not a member of the SRK command. I'm not familiar with this order. It does read what you say, but it never came about. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at Bascarsija after the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you say -- I'm a little confused. If you're saying that you don't know anything about something, but then at the same time you're claiming that it never happened, I'm confused how you could say both.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I saw Bascarsija right after the war. Nothing was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not part of the command at that time, and I couldn't have seen this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I became a corps command member in 1995. I don't know anything about this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if you say that the one contradicts the other, and that I tend to disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because you can not know anything about an order being given and, nevertheless, to establish that what you've seen in your life is inconsistent with the execution of such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a possibility. The witness explained that. But when you put the question, I thought you could have already in an attempt to properly understand the witness, you might have come to that thought already. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's understood. Your Honour, I'm actually going to move on to another document. I don't know if this is a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then perhaps it's better to take the break first. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Veljovic, and would like to see you back after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, while we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, may I take it that you'll easily finish within the next hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll try to make that easily within the next hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So I approximate about another 35 to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, Mr. Weber will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30811 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, this is a document that the Defence tendered through you in the Milosevic case. It is a 12 August 1994 order from SRK Commander Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to the last page of both versions of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Above the typewritten signature of this order, there are the initials DM. Is it correct that this indicates Dragomir Milosevic drafted this order himself?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it does say DM/UM. Most likely it is so, but I find it rather unlikely that the commander would draft a document himself. In any case, his name is not in the signature bloc.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. We understand that this was a dispatch that you had testified to before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to the first page of the B/C/S original but stay on the same page of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I seek a clarification. Mr. Veljovic, you said his name, and that was a reference to Dragomir Milosevic, his name doesn't appear in the signature bloc. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I find it strange that someone else signed the order and that Milosevic dictated it, although he was the corps commander. I don't know why someone else would sign it, but I may be oblivious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go back to the last page in B/C/S. Do you see a name in the signature bloc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Dragomir Milosevic. But there -- there -- he didn't sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is no signature to be seen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, excuse me, I might have been off on the -- the page. If we could go back to page 1 of the B/C/S and go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you said I would be surprised if one else signed for him. But there is no signature at all under the document, so I did not fully understand what you meant by someone else signing for him. Apart from that, that seems to be a telex-type communication, which is not equipped for signatures to be -- to be communicated. So I do not fully see what -- what you intend to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is strange that he may have dictated this document, that somebody else typed it, that there is his name in the signature bloc, and there is no signature. On the other hand, the heading is appropriately worded, and the document came from the command so all that is strange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If I could go -- please go to page 1 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English translation. And in the B/C/S, if we could please scroll down towards the bottom of the page. As with the same in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to item number 7. Under this item, General Milosevic orders: "Artillery anti-aircraft missile unit and armoured mechanised units to be on stand-by with necessary forces and equipment to act on targets on earth and in air-space."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, this is not exactly what we see on this English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I misread the order, Your Honour. I'll reread it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "Artillery anti-aircraft defence artillery and rocket units and armoured mechanised units to be on stand-by with necessary forces and equipment to act on targets on the ground and in the air-space." And then under the second indentation, it says: "4th Mixed Artillery Regiment is to draw up a fire plan in the region of Bascarsija and Vrbanja. Fire is to be opened according to the order from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Command Post." Sir, I put it to you that the SRK command did, in fact, issue orders for fire plans that targeted Bascarsija. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably that was the case. However, fire was not to be opened without his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders the document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30811 receives number P6606, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before I go on to another document, I just want to note: Do you understand the English language? Are you able to read or write it? Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30856. The B/C/S translation of this document is pending, so with Your Honours' leave, I'd just read out the sections to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see how much it is. And if you would please read slowly --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And if we could please scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, this is an UNPROFOR sitrep from Sector Sarajevo dated 21 March 1993. I'm going to read a few portions of this sitrep to you. If at any time you need me to repeat what I'm saying, please let me know. Under section 2, it says: "Response. I responded to Dr. Ganic as follows:" And then there is a subpart, a, that says "Shelling Activity." Under item 1, the sitrep says: "HQ Sector Sarajevo was well aware of the shelling activity in the old city. Military observers in observation posts overlooking the area had recorded the attacks."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And then I'd like to read one more portion to the witness. Could we please have page 2 of this sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under item 3, it states: "Investigation. The following investigative action was taken:" There is a subpart a. "Number of Impacts. A fair estimate of the number of artillery and mortar impacts recorded by the UNMOs in the old city area, from approx 0530 hours to approx 1000 hours on 21 Mar, is in excess of 400. While not a record, it is an unusually high number of impacts in this area. It should be noted that the total number of impacts recorded for the entire area under observation for today is 2398." Sir, I put it to you that Bascarsija, the old city, was in fact shelled, that at times it was heavily shelled, and it did cause destruction or damage to the Bascarsija area. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment. I was not a corps member at that time. I am not familiar with this order. I guarantee you that that didn't happen. The old city is a large area which belonged to both the Serbs and the Muslims; i.e., it was in -- under their control. It is Sedrenik, Bistrik, Bascarsija, Polog, Hresa, and it goes all the way to Vucija Luka [phoen]. All that is in the old city. When this happened, I don't know. I don't know who this order was sent to and when. In 1994, in the month of December, I was a corps member; therefore, I was never familiar with this particular order. If that many shells had ever fallen on the old city, they would have caused havoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders the document into evidence. We ask that it be MFI'd -- I'm sorry, Your Honours. The translation is not complete. If we could inform the Chamber when it is complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number assigned to this document would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30856 receives number P6607, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pending translation, P6607 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to move on to another topic. And before I show you something, I'm just going to explain you something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I'm a bit concerned and a bit worried by a possible misunderstanding. The English texts here relates to "the old city area." Now you have not explained that much why -- whether the old city area is the same as Bascarsija, or whether Bascarsija is part of that old city. Well, that would need more attention to know exactly whether Bascarsija was targeted. But there is another matter. The witness says that the old city area was, to some extent, even under Serb control, which makes me fear that he has a totally different understanding and that Stari Grad, which means the old town, which may not be the city centre itself, that there is some confusion caused by the difference in language as well which has not been clarified until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, I understand your concern. And I think at least what would be relevant for the testimony of the witness is to get his understanding, and I'm happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He gave -- he gave some of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said that the old city area was partly under Serb control, and you just moved to your next subject. So if you say "seeking that," I mean, the witness hinted at it, but you apparently did not catch it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I am not sure where we're at. Would you like me to ask a -- is there something that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I've explained to you what my concerns are and the evidence that you are eliciting at this moment, so it's up to you to see whether you can make any clearer and how to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do you consider Bascarsija a part of the old city?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one part of it is part of the old city. The entire area of Sedrenik, the entire area of Bistrik, and both were under the control of the Muslim forces. Our parts were Hresa, Bolazi [phoen] and one part of Trebevic. The inhabited part of Trebevic; several villages there. And the entire residential area of the old city was under the control of the Muslim forces. We're talking about the municipality of Stari Grad, which is quite spacious.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. With that, sir, I'm going to move on to another topic. In the Karadzic case, the Office of the Prosecutor was provided with two statements from you. These two statements are almost the same in substance. The one that was tendered and admitted in this case as D532 has a few additional paragraphs. Paragraph 2 of the admitted statement in this case states: "I testified in the case of Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic," and provides the case number. This paragraph was different from your other Karadzic statement which has not been tendered, which is what I'd now like to discuss with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30805.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This document are two B/C/S texts under this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution apologises for that. I do have the English in front of me. If I -- I can read it and then we could replace it, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there is any way you could get it on the screen, if it's uploaded under any other number, then we would like to see it. Because the Chamber is usually inclined to follow also in reading what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course. It was the copy that was filed with the 92 ter motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we may have that before us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to paragraph 2 of your other Karadzic statement, it states: "At the beginning of the interview, I was shown a summary of the transcript of my testimony before the Tribunal" -- excuse me, "testimony before the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague in case," and there is IT-98-29/1-T, "I hereby confirm its contents and add the following." Mr. Veljovic, do you confirm that this is what happened during your interview with the Karadzic Defence?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you go on reading? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you can look at paragraph 2 of the -- of your other statement in front of us, can you confirm that that is what happened during your interview with the Karadzic Defence?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, there is no recorded interpretation. Did you provide an answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness did but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say anything. I just read that I testified in The Hague, before the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague in the case IT-98-29/1-T. I hereby confirm its contents and add the following. I'm a timber technician, that's under number 3, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. The question by Mr. Weber was whether you were, indeed, shown a summary of the transcript of your testimony in the case mentioned and whether you then confirmed the content of that. Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably it was shown to me. I don't remember at the moment. I only remember the case designation, but I don't know what it refers to, what case we're talking about. What does the number stand for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the Dragomir Milosevic case? Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Weber, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that should have been -- if you would have said that immediately. Well, the question is whether the Karadzic Defence lawyers, or the Defence team, whether they had shown you a summary of the testimony you had given in the Dragomir Milosevic case and whether you then confirmed its contents and then added other things. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't ask me much about Milosevic before I came to testify in the Mladic case. They just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- gave me some outlines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who -- who -- one second, please. When you say, "they just gave me some outline," who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor asked me something about the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly what. I don't know what he asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let's go back. This is a statement which was given to the Karadzic Defence, and it states that at the beginning of the interview - that is, the interview with the Karadzic Defence, not the Mladic Defence but the Karadzic Defence - that at the beginning of the interview, you were shown - that is, on paper - a summary of the testimony you had given in the Milosevic case and that you then said, "Well, I confirm the content of what you just have shown me." Is that what happened, when preparing for your Karadzic testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't show me this IT-98-29/1-T. They didn't show it to me. They just asked me questions in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, one question for you. You -- this is what you produced. What summary was shown to the witness, as far as the Mladic Defence is concerned? I mean, the witness confirms a summary, which is apparently not a full transcript of his Dragomir Milosevic Defence [sic], so the Chamber would be interested to know what was shown to him and ask you whether you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to tell you what I did with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you what the Karadzic Defence team did with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stop. You present to us this material as relevant for our decision-making, so I'm not asking you what you did, but I'm asking you what summary was shown to the witness by the Karadzic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I learned from Witness Veljovic was that when -- before he testified in the Karadzic case, the Karadzic Defence team told him -- or, rather, reminded him and briefly reminded him of how he testified in the Milosevic case. They asked him if he wanted to stick by that testimony, he confirmed, but that he also wishes to add something. After having received such an answer from Mr. Veljovic, this Defence team learned that Mr. Veljovic has other things to add before he came to testify, and that's what we added to his previous statement to which he fully adheres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you did not immediately inform everyone that where it says that the witness was shown a summary, which he confirms, which is quite an important matter, that that, in fact, had not been done, and that he was just orally -- and that you did not even know. You didn't verify with the Karadzic Defence. You just let us read that the witness was shown a summary, and that's what you want to present as evidence. Not knowing what the summary was, even thinking that there was no written summary at all that could have been shown to him. That's apparently the situation. I can't -- I can't find anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My conclusion precisely, Your Honours. The witness told us that he was reminded of what he said, that the transcript was verbally presented to him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in a shortened form. I don't know what else the Karadzic Defence team did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Stojanovic, that's now the second time you tell us, and I've heard that, but that contradicts what is in a statement you present to us as evidence. Because the statement says, "I was shown a summary." Therefore, my question: Where is the summary? So that we know at least what the witness would have confirm. Then you say there was no summary, at least no written summary; and, at the same time, you present in evidence that there was a written summary. That is, at the best, sloppy. Let's leave it to that. Mr. Weber -- well, if you want to add anything, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, I take note of what you're saying. In the statement, it says clearly that there are no written transcripts. It says here, in the B/C/S version, at the beginning of the interview: "I was confronted with the summary of the transcript," and this is what the witness told us, but he did -- he wasn't shown a written, a full written transcript. The witness never told us that. The Karadzic Defence team just confronted him with the outlines of the transcript. It doesn't say in the B/C/S version that the witness was ever shown a written summary of the transcript, or the full transcript for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, when I use strong wordings, if there is a translation issue, which could have been clear if the Prosecution would have uploaded both the B/C/S and the English version of this, then we would have identified that. Because in English it doesn't say "I was shown the transcript" or "I was" -- if you say "I was shown," that means you can look at it. Well, you can't look at words. You can only look at objects and that would be a text. But if the original says, "I was confronted with a summary of my Dragomir Milosevic testimony," then it may well be that the translation does not reflect what the original says.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour, in the first manner, we have corrected the upload. We do have that available now as 65 ter 30805a. And, Your Honours, thank you for your indulgence on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So with respect to the second matter, I don't how else to actually reconcile that except to ask for some type of verification or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have to -- it's certain that the translation of paragraph 2, and then especially the first sentence of this document, should be verified by CLSS. Mainly focusing on whether -- well, I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if I was use -- again, if I use strong words, and if it's due to a translation error, then I apologise for that. But, unfortunately, I cannot work but in the language I master. And apparently you have the same problem as far as your language is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't hold it against me, Your Honour. But, quite simply, I'm all tense myself, and I'm getting lost myself with all these three statements from three trials, and I cannot even remember all the things that I discussed with all these different people, so many of them, so I really do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, everyone is now at ease again. Mr. Weber, you as well? Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know you had a preference for not having multiple statements in, but the statement that is admitted is very similar to this statement. I've pointed out the main differential. I don't know if you want to mark it for identification, or just not have it, and then have an oral report at a later date as to the verification of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you first elicit the evidence and then we'll see what we might need on the record. If there are small portions to be read, it's fine. If it's longer portions we'll have to look at, then we might find other solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, is it correct that the contents of your statements, both of them, in the Karadzic case were additions to matters that you did not mention during your testimony in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it certainly does contain what I did not mention during the Milosevic case, but you see how this goes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone and could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were invited to come closer to the microphone, Mr. Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in the Karadzic case, at transcript page 29262, you were asked about your previous testimony in the Milosevic case. You were asked the following: "Q. And when you came here to testify in his defence, you knew what he was charged with at the time?" You answered: "Yes, I knew what he had been charged with." Do you stand by this testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not fully read his indictment, but I know what he was indicted for, the blockade of Sarajevo, shelling. I don't know all these things that were put forth by the Prosecutor. Sniping, killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you aware that General Milosevic was charged with the shelling of the Markale market-place on 28 August 1995 when you testified in his case?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he was charged for Markale, for what had happened on the 28th of August, but General Milosevic was not really commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps at that time. It was Cedo Sladoje. And I kept saying that time and again. And it wasn't taken into account until it was proven before the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you were aware of General Milosevic being charged with the shelling of the Markale market. The first line of your answer completely answers the question: You knew that he was charged for Markale. All the rest was not asked. Mr. Weber may have other questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you testified in the Milosevic case for four days?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were asked about your time in the 4th Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade during your Milosevic testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were specifically asked about the staffing level of the 4th Slpbr and the weapons you had?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During your Milosevic testimony, is it correct that you did not claim that two 120-millimetre mortars from the 4th Slpbr were redeployed from Trebevic to Trebinje in August 1995? This is just something you added for your testimony in the Karadzic case for the first time; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't have testified about that in the Milosevic case when they hadn't asked me about it. They didn't ask me about Markale at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there might be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Find it where they asked me about the Markale situation in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, my question wasn't about whether you were asked about the Markale market. You've already confirm that you were asked about the equipment you had and its deployments, its staffing level. So I want to stay and focus on that.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they asked me about the weapons, deployment, and personnel that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm happy to go through two pages of transcript from the Milosevic testimony. The witness has confirmed the fact that he did not discuss the specific things. I don't know if it's going to be -- if you want me to spend the time doing it, or if you would just -- I don't know if the Defence would have any objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- if I would just tender the two pages for the Chamber to be able to assess it on its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or agree that he did not address the matter. I mean, to read in those two pages to find out that the witness did not say in those two pages anything about the -- apparently the removal of certain equipment at a certain period of time and that he just testified about the equipment overall they had without referring to temporary absence of part of that equipment, I think the parties could agree on that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That would be fine. But it would also allow the Chamber to see that he was asked questions which may have triggered other information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if there are specific questions, you say, "Well, this should have" -- a complete answer would have required, then please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- either give them to us or agree with Mr. Stojanovic that we can read them, and then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is with pleasure that I will reach an agreement with the Prosecution on that. If the Prosecutor also agrees that this kind of question about units and artillery pieces of the brigade that was headed by the witness had not been put in that concrete case, then I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. If we agree that the transcript can come in, I believe the Chamber can assess it for itself as to what was asked and what was in the context of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently on -- I leave it to you whether you want to wait for the break and to see what you can agree upon with Mr. Stojanovic, or to start now, but the Chamber would not be -- would not highly appreciate to hear an oral recitation of two pages of a document mainly to find out what is not in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Find a suitable way of resolving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 30 of your statement, admitted as D532, you claim that your brigade, the 4th Slpbr, had a mortar battery with two 120-millimetre mortars in the Brus sector. Is it correct that this sector is on the eastern portion of Mount Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But it's not the eastern portion of Mount Trebevic, it's the central portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 31, you claim that your mortar battery and 160 men were sent to the Trebinje front around the 24th of August, 1995. Do I understand correctly that it is your evidence that you sent two 120-millimetre mortars and six 82-millimetre mortars to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly that the 160 men and the mortar battery were the only support that you sent to the Herzegovina Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those 160 men were not mine. Perhaps 80 were mine, and the rest is from the sabotage detachment from the corps. And my deputy was appointed commander of that unit - Kojic, Radomir - to go and help the Herzegovina Corps. Since he led that unit, he took his own resources because he trusted his own resources as support, and he took these mortars and took his own unit because he had full support -- he had full confidence that they would support him the best. And I reacted and I called Cedo at that time because Cedo was the commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir -- sir, I'm sorry to cut you off. I wasn't asking for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if we could please go through this in an orderly fashion and please listen to my questions. Is what you described in your statement and in -- in just your answer just now, the only support that you sent to the Herzegovina Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only support that was sent by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: These weapons from the battery were no longer available to your brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Until it returned from the area of Trebinje. In the month of September, around the middle of the month, it returned from Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that you left your positions on the Trebevic axis undefended at the end of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we left them undefended as far as my brigade was concerned. However, the corps gave me approval for the corps artillery to support me because the mortars of the other battalions were far away. Gorazde, the Nisici plateau, I did not have any battalions nearby. The brigade was deployed towards Gorazde, the Jahorina Battalion towards Olovo, and the Trebevic Battalion towards the city of Sarajevo. Since, at Borije, there was a mixed artillery regiment, that regiment could have supported me at any point in time. There wasn't any combat, and I never asked for any support because the offensive was practically over, and the army was at peace. There weren't any provocations coming from the Muslims, so I had no need to use the artillery. If it was necessary, then I would have called the corps, and the corps group would support me from Borije.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did the corps artillery take up your positions on Mount Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, and they helped me many times. Not the entire corps artillery but part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30809.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While that comes up, Mr. Weber, could you please look at line 21 on page 44. I just want to clarify, did you ask: "Did the corps artillery take up your positions" or "their positions"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for catching that. I believe I said "did the corps artillery take up your positions on Mount Trebevic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was your intention to say "your positions".

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. I think that the question is a confusing one and not precise. What does that mean, "to take over positions"? Physically or by artillery fire? I think it would be fairer to the witness to put the question in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can do so in re-examination, Mr. Stojanovic. At least taking a position is, for me, clear language, but if there is any doubt about that, please explore that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution -- I believe, actually -- yup, the document is before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for what you said and what the Prosecutor said just now: None of that has been interpreted. I see General Mladic reacting to that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I re-read it so that Mr. Mladic is able to hear it. Mr. Stojanovic, you raised the issue about the unclarity of the question and thought it would be fairer to the witness to put the question in a different way. Then I said: "You can do so in re-examination, Mr. Stojanovic. At least taking a position is, for me, clear language, but if there is any doubt about that, please explore that later on." And then Mr. Weber said: "Could the Prosecution -- I believe, actually -- yup, the document is before us." That's what he said. And then you intervened. The record being complete now again, please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. For the record, before us on the screen is 65 ter 30809.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, this is a 17 August 1995 4th Slpbr report on the state of combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this report is from you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. My signature is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please return to the first page of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this first page, under section (a), your report states: "The brigade is stretched along the front carrying out its combat tasks along the following three axes: Nisici, Trebevic, and Praca." Is it correct that your brigade was still active on the Trebevic axis as of this date?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, with one battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, the report states: "Even though the brigade had barely got to its feet, it was immediately thrown into the fire, and 100 troops were engaged on the Trebinje axis and 70 troops on the Trnovo front, making the already wide zone of responsibility even more vulnerable." Sir, I put it to you that contrary to your statement that, in fact, you had already sent 100 troops to the Herzegovina Corps by the 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what I said. Earlier on, the 23rd, 24th. So I sent them earlier to the Herzegovina Corps, August, before the situation in Markale took place, and that is what I reported too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this part of your report makes no reference to the sending of a mortar battery? It simply states 100 troops were engaged on the Trebinje axis.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the commander on the Trebinje axis was Commander Kojic, my deputy, who asked for support. One hundred men of mine and Srdjan's from the Sabotage Detachment. And he asked for resources by way of support, and the corps didn't give him any, and he said that he would take his own from Trebevic and that the corps should take care of supporting me rather than bringing weapons to my positions where the mortars were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it's break time. I do have more questions on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, and we'll resume - after the witness has left the courtroom - at 10 minutes past 12.00.
