utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom, any news?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we did have a discussion with the Defence over the course of the break, and I believe it's the agreement between the parties that two pages of Mr. Veljovic's previous Milosevic transcript could be admitted. These pages being page 5834 and -35 from those proceedings. The Prosecution is in the process of uploading those materials under 65 ter number 30807a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once that's done, please inform the Chamber so that we can decide on admission. Mr. Stojanovic, I take it that you -- Mr. Weber has presented your agreement accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. May I just confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions of the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, I'd like to direct your attention to the middle of the page in the B/C/S, the part that states: "We are unable to form:" In the paragraph right underneath that, there is a discussion of fire support platoons in the infantry companies. Do you see this section of your report?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this section makes no reference to the lack of 120-millimetre mortars in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the order arrived from the corps to establish a group of people consisting of 106 combatants and that they should be sent to the front line in Trebinje, I formed a group of 60 men and that included support. These 70 men I sent to Trebinje are from the platoons of mortars of 82 millimetres, 120 millimetres, and also the assault platoon that I had. And the other men were from the 10th Sabotage --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Detachment of Srdjan Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, please listen to my questions, and you -- you've already stated that. My question was just simply that there's no reference in this section to the lack of 120-millimetre mortars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could not establish a battery because six weapons are needed for that, and we had only two. And those two were sent with the 82s to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. The question was whether the report explains what you apparently want to explain to us. Does it say anything about mortars not being there? That's the question. 120 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could you read this out for me, please? I cannot see it very well. Can you tell me what is written there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the report is about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you want me to read this section --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the combat readiness. But we did not find anything on the relocation or the removal of mortars, even if temporarily. And we are not going to read the entire document for you to find out that it isn't there. If there is any relevant portion, Mr. Stojanovic in re-examination, will deal with the matter. Please proceed Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, at the end of this section, immediately above the words "logistical support," your report states that the brigade staffing level is at 89 per cent, and in parentheses, it says it should have 1.732 men and it has 1.568 men. Is this information accurate?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 30809 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is not 30807a? No. It's 08. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 30809 will be P6608.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6608 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30808. And if we could please just go up briefly in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 31 August 1995 listing from the command of the 4th Slpbr which lists, according to the first sentence above the listing of the munitions: "Pursuant to your request," then there is a number, "we hereby submit the availability of ammunition and fuel to the brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please go to the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this document is from you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct that it is my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under item number 11, it relates to mortar 120 mm M 75, and then going across it says "arms availability," and says 13. Sir, I put it to you that even after you sent men to Trebinje that you had 120 -- that you had at least 13 120-millimetre mortars available to you in your brigade.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I had 13 120-millimetre pieces; two in Trebevic, six at the Nisic plateau, which is 50 kilometres away from Sarajevo; and the rest of the mortars were in the direction of Gorazde. I couldn't have taken anything from the Igman and Podrinje Battalions in order to have more mortars, and I also included on this list the number of mortars which went to Trebinje. They, too, belonged to my unit, and they were supposed to return eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 30808 will be P6609.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to report that the two transcript pages have now been uploaded. I know Mr. Stojanovic still needs time. But with that, the Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, could you please repeat the number under which now the two pages are uploaded and assign a number to them so that they can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the two pages have been uploaded under 30807a, and they receive number P60 -- 6610.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this document is admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, usually transcript pages are not translated. If there would be any specific need to have them translated here, but I would suggest to you that since the main purpose is to find out what is not on those pages, that perhaps exceptionally we could do without. But we would like to hear from you if you take a different position. Then, Mr. Veljovic, if Mr. Stojanovic has any further questions for you, he'll re-examine you now. Mr. Stojanovic -- but perhaps I -- before I give you an opportunity to do that, we have looked at the combat readiness, we have looked at a document about availability of ammunition and fuel, all in order to establish whether the mortars were relocated, were sent elsewhere in August 1995, yes or no. Now, the orders, as you said, were ordered to send them to the Trebinje front, were they in writing or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a corps command, which was oral, because the corps could not support assets. Then they said that they could provide corps support for our battalion from their positions and that our mortars go to the Trebinje theater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I would like to know is whether there is any written order saying, "You move your mortars to Trebinje" or "to" -- whether there were any written orders either to the -- going down to the mortar crews who would transport them, or orders coming from the higher level? Because I do understand that they were -- they were sent to Trebinje to assist the Herzegovina Corps, which is another corps, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But now any written trace of those orders, either coming down from the corps level or between the two corps or being sent down to the levels where it had to be executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there was a corps order to assign a number of personnel to Trebinje. They also stipulated who was to be commander. It was my Chief of Staff, Major Gojic, to accompany the men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was that in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 100 per cent. Cedo Sladoje was the commander at the time, and his deputy was the -- was Lizdek, Vlado, who was the commander of the 1st Romanija Brigade, given the fact that Milosevic underwent an operation at the time. Since he had been operated on, someone else had to be appointed as acting Chief of Staff by the Main Staff commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did it say anything about the equipment to be taken, mortars? You earlier told us that you do not easily move a mortar from one place to another. Was there any mentioning of that in those orders? Or that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That had not been ordered. It was said that units needed corps artillery support, but the corps was in no position to do so. Given that Radomir was in command of the Trebevic Battalion, it was ordered that he would take the assets to the Trebevic theater of war. He took our assets, and Cedo said, "Well, you don't need them anyway because we can give support to your unit at any point in time from Borije from our positions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stop, stop --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are both written and oral orders in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any written order which specifically deals with the transfer of the mortars, the 120-millimetre mortars, to the Trebinje front in order to assist the Herzegovina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. I think there must be a corps order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because that would be logical, you would say. You wouldn't do that without having a corps order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The parties --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander could also issue an oral order saying, "Give him those assets, and I will provide support for you instead."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties are invited, to the extent possible, to find any written trace of such a transfer of mortar equipment. Then, Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just two things before I put my first question. Line 19, page 53 of the temporary transcript, the witness mentioned a name of the person who assumed the duty of commanding the unit. However, we only have the last name recorded incorrectly. I can repeat the first and last name, but perhaps it's better for the witness to say so, so that we know the name of his Chief of Staff who went to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radomir Kojic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Before Mr. Stojanovic begins with his questions, the interpreter kindly asks that the pauses between questions and answers be strictly observed, given the witness's speed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, your special attention is requested to take a break after the answer of the witness because the witness is speaking at such a speed that the interpreters really need time and that you, therefore, should wait a moment before you put your next question to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have -- actually, while this document is still before us, Your Honour, I have one question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Veljovic, you see the document before you dated the 31st of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In item 11, you inform the command of the SRK that in your brigade there is a total of 13 120-millimetre pieces.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the figure of 13 include the two pieces sent to the Trebinje theater of war?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second. Witness, could you also have a small pause between question and answer because the interpreters couldn't hear your answer. Could you answer the question again, whether those two sent to Trebinje were included in the 13 listed here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were included, given the fact that the unit was supposed to return to its original unit. I had to have them included in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Stojanovic, may I ask for another clarification. You asked for the full name of the deputy, and the witness said Radomir Kojic, as it is recorded. Before that, he said it was Major Gojic. I would like to ask the witness which of the two names is correct: Kojic or Gojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kojic, with a K.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the one question you said you had for the witness, Mr. Stojanovic, was answered already by him in -- on page 51, line -- I think it's 19. "And I also included on the list the number of mortars which was sent to Trebinje." So that question had been answered. You asked it again, you got the same answer. You had one question, you said, to the witness, but I'll remind you, perhaps after the third or the fourth, that you had only one. Please proceed. Well, we live in the reality that one question sometimes amounts to two or three, or sometimes even four, and I'll remind you about that later. But this one question was superfluous. Please now a relevant question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we have in e-court document P6604, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, the second paragraph of item 5 reads: "Two AB launchers to be prepared" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- "for action against the elevation" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to move to the next page. We are there now. Please, let me just see what you read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the heading of the document, we see that the date is the 10th of August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now go back to page 2 again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not with the corps at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Regardless of the fact that you were not with the corps at the time, do you have any knowledge about whether there was any use of air bombs against the features mentioned therein?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the fact that you are a reserve officer, did you ever receive any specialist training in ballistics?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I did command a mortar platoon with 82-millimetres which used as a part of the battalion artillery support group. That was back in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, did you at any point in time have any direct contact with the preparation and manufacturer of modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever. I am not an expert, and I did not work with metal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the approximate range of modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I may have picked it up along the way, but I'm not sure. I have never read the rules. I don't know what the range is. Perhaps up to 5 kilometres. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Given the extent of your knowledge, can you tell us what happens if one of the rocket engines mounted on an air bomb fails to ignite?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not any significant range to speak of, and of course it would be diverted to the side of the engine which did not start.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the repair institute in Hadzici, given the fact that was a multi-purpose production factory, produced or manufactured launchers on the basis of stands otherwise used for artillery?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Grad rockets do have their own tables of firing?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell the Court whether, in the SRK, there were multiple rocket launchers such as the Oganj?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the mixed artillery regiment they did have such launchers, although I don't know what kind they were. They may have had the Oganj or the Plamen. Bartula also had some mounted on a vehicle, but I'm not privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it a very efficient and lethal asset?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is extremely lethal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. It's leading. Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the objection? Leading. Mr. Stojanovic, could you please refrain from leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, to the extent of your knowledge, what kind of assets it is and what are its possibilities?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its possibilities are enormous. It can cover a very large area with its fire-power. It used to be produced in our multi-purpose production factories, including all the tests it had to undergo. It included the multiple rocket-launchers of Oganj, Plamen, and Orkan. However, I'm not familiar with any technical details in terms of firing, use, et cetera. I just know they can cover a very wide area and are particularly lethal when it comes to infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were such assets used at any point in time on the military targets in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as I know, they were not used since 1993, when they were excluded. In order for anyone to use such weapons, UNPROFOR must have been notified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Veljovic, for your answers and for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. At the same time, for the Chamber to fully understand the last portion of your examination, we are a bit lost about how details of other armament would shed any light on the air bombs issue. But perhaps you can explain us after the witness has left the courtroom because we are -- And I have one other question for you, which is: These locations mentioned as where the air bombs should be directed at when on standby, the Chamber has not heard what kind of positions they are. The witness explained to us that it was just wasteland, nothing there, and the Chamber would like to ask the parties to see whether they can agree on, first of all, where it is, and if it's really empty space there, inaccessible, if you would agree on that, the Chamber would like to know that. If you do not agree on it, the Chamber would like to agree as well. Or if you want to present further evidence on the type of terrain which is meant in this document. No further questions, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Veljovic, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well, Mr. President, and thank you, Judges, as well as everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojcic, Vladimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a preliminary matter with this witness, it is the Prosecution's position that he probably should receive a warning under 90(E). He received it in the Karadzic case. There is an extensive rules of the road file regarding him, and he does acknowledge that he issued the order to fire the air bomb into Hrasnica which is G10 in this indictment. So I think, given everything, it is -- it would be appropriate that he be given that warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic requested the Defence [sic] not to repeat these kind of things. At the same time, Mr. Lukic, you are the one who has asked for certain orders, which makes it a bit surprising that you objected so much to what -- what the Prosecution did. We leave it in your hands as always.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for this particular witness, I leave it in the hands of Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He's more familiar with that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would suggest, Your Honours, I have no objection to the 90(E) warning being given at the beginning of the witness's evidence. That was what was done in the Karadzic case. And I -- although I don't think that the answers and the questions that I'm going through will raise anything, it's better to perhaps cover the whole ambit of possible testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll take care of that. Good morning -- good afternoon, yes, I'm corrected by my colleagues. Mr. Radojcic, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojcic, before you'll be examined, I would like to bring the following to your attention. You as a witness, you may object to answer any question if the answer to that question might tend to incriminate yourself. Although we have the possibility to compel you to answer that question, that also would have certain consequences as to whether then your answer could be used in a subsequent prosecution against yourself for any offence. But so if at any time you think that a truthful answer is at risk to incriminate yourself, you may ask not to be obliged to answer that question. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear to me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you'll first be examined now by Mr. Ivetic. You find him to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please first state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: My name is Vladimir Radojcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to first call up 65 ter number 1D01625. And with the assistance of the usher, I also have a hard copy that should be shown to the Prosecution first and given to the witness for ease of going through the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if I can direct your attention to the signature that appears on the first page of the original, can you confirm for us if that is your signature that appears there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to review this statement in the Serbian language during proofing subsequent to having signed the same?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you have some corrections to the statement which you told me about in proofing?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Well, I made the first correction on the front page because my date of birth has been misrecorded. Later on, while reading the statement, I noticed two other minor mistakes that do not affect my statement significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll take them each in turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could first turn to page 11 in the English and page 14 in the Serbian, and it'll -- it'll leak on to the top of page 15. And I think the text that we're talking about is at the top of page 15 in relation to paragraph 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, is the average deviation for an aerial bomb accurately stated in this paragraph as being 10 to 1.000 metres?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian version of this statement of mine, it is correct; that is to say, it was from 10 metres to 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat what's been translated: Is it correct to say that the deviation was from 10 metres to 1.000 metres?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please state what the deviation for an aerial bomb should be, according to your information.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: This deviation should be interpreted in the following way: The deviation was, on average, 10 metres for 1.000 metres, a distance of 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to paragraph 63 which is on page 12 in the English and page 16 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is there anything that needs to be corrected in this paragraph, paragraph 63? And I would direct your attention to the English version of the same, so you can compare the information contained in the English and the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian version, the information is correct, that my wife worked until the 2nd of May, 1992. In the English version, it is 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the translation we received, we heard "2nd of May, 1992." Is that what, in fact, you meant?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to paragraph 110, which is on page 18 in the English and page 24 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, this would be at paragraph 110. Do you have any corrections to make to any of the information or dates contained in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: It is the 26th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, the date is the same in the English version and in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is that date accurate, according to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, apart from the changes or clarifications that we've gone through, do you affirm that everything in your statement is accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you the same questions today about the same topics as contained in your statement, would your answers be the same, in substance?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now that you have taken the solemn declaration, would those answers as contained in this statement be truthful?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would move to admit 1D01625 as the next available Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D01625 receives number D535.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At this time, Your Honours, I would like to read a public summary of the statement, the purposes of which have been explained to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Vladimir Radojcic was a colonel in the VRS, and he was commander of the 1st Infantry Ilidza Brigade of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps from January 1993 through the end of the war. He was a professional army officer, but his brigade had a serious manpower problem, and only one other officer, the artillery commander, had been a professional army officer prior to the war. This lack of professional officers was similar in other brigades. Colonel Radojcic was aware of the formation of the Green Berets on the Muslim side as an armed formation before the war. These units were armed with new equipment and weapons. Colonel Radojcic often complained to the UN that the ABiH was using civilian facilities for military activities. Before opening fire on a civilian area used by the ABiH, the VRS would warn the UN to warn the other side. The territory of his brigade was fired upon from the Dobrinja hospital, among other civilian areas being used by the ABiH. The strategy of the SRK was to protect civilian villages and prevent a breakthrough of the ABiH 1st Corps situated in Sarajevo. The Ilidza Brigade undertook primarily defensive operations toward that strategy. The only offensive operations were to improve tactical positions. His brigade opened fire at the first line of the front and targeted the depth of Sarajevo only when they had reliable information that combat elements of the ABiH were located there. The VRS Main Staff and Sarajevo Romanija Corps provided manuals and ordered that they be distributed to subordinates, detailing the laws of war and calling for adherence to the same. His superiors in the corps and the Main Staff never ordered the brigade to attack civilians or civilian transportation lines in Sarajevo. The VRS Main Staff gave explicit orders to eliminate paramilitaries from the area, and the brigade undertook to try and implement those orders. The issue of ammunition became a problem, such that the superior commands issued orders to save ammunition and only fire upon the enemy when absolutely necessary. This ammunition problem led to the use of so-called modified aerial bombs, which were only used after they were tested and their precision ascertained. The witness knows the ABiH also used modified aerial bombs, including naval bombs. The witness testified about humanitarian aid being allowed to pass, even though it was known that the ABiH in Sarajevo misappropriated the same and sold it on the black market. He is aware of instances where UN and UNPROFOR vehicles were smuggling weapons and munitions to the ABiH in Sarajevo. As to Scheduled Incident G10, Colonel Radojcic states that this was fired at a legitimate military target. As to Scheduled Incident G6, Colonel Radojcic states that his forces did not have mortars at the institute for the blind, and he issued no orders to fire upon Klare Cetkin Street. As to Incidents G13 and G15, Colonel Radojcic never instructed or ordered those locations to be attacked, nor received reports of them being struck by his forces. And that, Your Honours, completes the summary of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would move to admit the associated exhibits that are contained in the statement which have not been already introduced into evidence. By my tally, there are 61 such exhibits that do not already have exhibit numbers. And I could either give a list now or perhaps sit with Mr. Groome at the break and show him my list to save -- to be more efficient. I'm at Your Honours' guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I take it that Mr. Groome has the list. And what I would like to know is whether there are any objections against any of those documents so that we could perhaps deal with the non-objected ones, and then we'll further hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to suggest that we do this at the end of the witness's testimony. I have a number of questions about some of them, and I believe there is some confusion which I will bring out during my cross-examination a bit. Depending on the answers, I will be either objecting or not objecting to the admission of some of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we leave the associated exhibits for a while and revisit the issue at the end of the testimony of the witness. Any questions for the witness, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Ivetic? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to ask you some follow-up questions. First, I would like to take a look at what you say in paragraph 7 of your statement, which has now been identified as Exhibit D535.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that would be page 3 in both language versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you say that the strategy of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was to utilise a "decisive defence." What precisely do you mean by the terminology "decisive defence"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Blocking defence, "odsudna odbrana," in military terminology means the defence of certain zones, areas, even if a maximum sacrifice is to be made in order to defend that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you say "even if a maximum sacrifice is to be made," what does that relate to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: First of all, I mean one's own losses in this case. When there is this kind of defence, there is no going back. This is the situation that the Ilidza Brigade was in because our families were behind our backs. That is why this defence is called that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, in this paragraph you state that your objective was to block the BH Army 1st Corps in the city. Was it also part of your objective to blockade civilians in the city of Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: No. In all the orders that I received from the superior commands, from the Main Staffs, it was always stated explicitly that our aim is to blockade the 1st Corps of the BH Army because it was so numerous that they could seriously threaten stability in other areas. As for the total blockade of Sarajevo, there was no mention of any such thing. On the contrary, we were always co-operative, and we always allowed civilians to leave. All our politicians, all our military leaders in negotiations always included that possibility as well; that is to say, allowing civilians to leave Sarajevo freely and come back to Sarajevo freely. However, the other side, in this case the 1st Corps of the BH Army, did not allow that. Or they set certain conditions that we did not find acceptable. That is to say, throughout the war, this was a pending issue, and we were always co-operative. And our co-operation with UNPROFOR units, and they were the mainstays of these negotiations, it was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How would you describe your own position, the position of your brigade vis-à-vis the ABiH forces that you were in contact with?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: The 1st Ilidza Infantry Brigade had combat contact with three brigades on the other side: The 102nd Brigade -- first, it was called the 2nd Brigade, but in the second stage of the war, it was renamed the 102nd Brigade, and it was in the inner ring of defence of the Brigade; then the 155th Brigade that was in the area of Dobrinja; and the 104th Brigade from Butmir near the runway of Sarajevo airport towards Hrasnica. It got to Igman and the source of the Bosna River. And that was where the area of responsibility of my brigade ended. And there were three, therefore, brigades on the other side. When I was looking at the balance of power between the two, it was 3:1 in their favour. Even 5:1 in their favour. So it was exceptionally difficult, an exceptionally difficult position, especially if you take into account the actual terrain that also worked in favour of our opposing side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now ask you about paragraph 5 of your statement, which is found in page 4 in the English and page 5 in the Serbian. Here you describe certain brochures explaining the provisions of international war and humanitarian laws distributed to subordinates. Can you describe to us, or tell us in more detail, about what kind of material was contained in these brochures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Ivetic, paragraph 5. I think you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 15, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should be page 5 in the Serbian, that's perhaps where I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give the following answer in response to your question. In these brochures, international law of war was explained and also what the units that are in conflict are supposed to do in order to observe that. Specific cases were referred to in terms of what violations of the law of war are. Literally, every soldier of the Ilidza Brigade and of the other forces of the 1st Corps was fully made aware, in detail, of these provisions of international law of war. If we take into account that in every order we got from General Mladic and from General Galic and General Milosevic, this was always underlined: The need to observe international law of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Turning to the brochures just for a moment, could you describe the level of sophistication of the language used in the brochures?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Well we, the officers, did our best to explain this to soldiers at our meetings. I told commanders of units within the brigade about this and then they would convey that to each and every soldier. We were even getting to be boring, if I can put it that way, with all of that. People were even saying enough with this international law of war. Why do you tell the other side about this, too, so that they start observing it a bit as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned meetings. Could you tell us about the frequency of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Well, most often I had briefings with my subordinate commanders once a week concerning problems in the brigade and they in their units. At the end of these meetings, we would adopt specific conclusions and tasks related to resolving these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are. Could you give us an indication as to how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I anticipate finishing in approximately 25 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think your initial claim was 30 minutes, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we are after half an hour now. Well, including -- well, not entirely half an hour, but including the attestations, et cetera, which is always understood to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have about 23 or 24 minutes -- 24 questions left, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll see how much time that takes. We ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00. And then you would be encouraged, Mr. Ivetic, to see whether you could finish by 2.00, let's say, that's almost the entire amount of time you asked for in total. So we take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Mladic is supposed not to speak aloud, not now, not at any time. Apart from that, I would like to previously address the parties on the following matter. Late September, two days in early October of this year, in total five days, we'll have to manoeuvre in such a way that the use of the courtrooms is in line with the staffing facilities, at least during the hearing of certain appeals. We always made an effort to secure that we would sit in the morning and would continue to sit in the morning because that was the expressed wish of the Defence. It may be that during those five days, in order to guarantee that we sit in the morning, we would have to start at 9.00. That's half an hour earlier than we usually do. It would be limited to those days only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is strong opposition to that, and the Chamber is inclined, rather, to stick to the morning sessions rather than to start at 9.30 or 9.00, the Chamber would like to hear without delay. Mr. Ivetic, please continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, now I would like to ask you about the procedure your brigade would follow when targeting enemy sites with mortar or artillery. First, could you tell me how targets on the enemy side were selected and identified?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not getting a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a minute. There seems to be a -- there seems to be a problem with the audio. Mr. Mladic, does it function now again or not yet? Yes, I see thumbs-up, which means we can proceed. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you start from the beginning so we could get the complete answer.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: In the brigade's operative room, there was a map which was used by the chief of artillery. All the targets where depicted on the map, those that were of some interest for the brigade, as well as the targets they'd receive from the corps command. They bore numbers, and they represented the targets on which we opened fire when needed. The corps command was in charge of some targets, and if they were in our area of responsibility -- responsibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- we did not open artillery fire on those targets because there was no need to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite you to slow down so that nothing of what you say will be lost. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you finish your question -- answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I wanted to add that those targets, which were marked on our map but were the responsibility of the corps artillery, were fired upon by the corps artillery, whereas the brigade artillery, the company artillery, and the battalion artilleries opened fire as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did your brigade heavy weapons have optical visibility with the targets on the other side?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: When we selected firing positions for the brigade firing group, I was guided by the following motive: Artillery had to be placed in such positions and deployed in such a way that they had optical visibility with the targets of my artillery. Since we also had laser gauges of a distance, the activity of our artillery tools was very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by "laser gauges of distance."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about a device using laser beams in order to measure the exact distance to the target. With that device, errors are really minimum, and they are measured in centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to look at paragraph 33 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Found on page 7 in the English and page 10 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I ask one clarifying question in relation to the previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "... errors are really minimum, and they are measured in centimetres." You mean errors in measuring the distance or any other error?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean distances, exclusively distances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, then I understood you well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this paragraph, paragraph 33, you say that you would alert the other side when firing at military targets of the ABiH in civilian zones through the UN. Could you describe how this was accomplished.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: In my brigade's zone of responsibility, there were military observers, and there were also UNPROFOR members. Throughout the war, the French Foreign Legion members were deployed there, as well as members of the Ukraine Battalion. There was a liaison officer in each of our brigades. With their help, we would very quickly get in contact with them, and whenever there was a violation of a truce or some other violation, we would inform them. When we did that, they would come to the scene to see what had happened, and then they would use their communications means in order to alert their colleagues on the other side who would then make sure that the offending activity was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it always the case that the offending activity was stopped?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: No, not always. Sometimes their fire continued, and then upon receiving approval from the superior command we would respond to that fire and neutralise their activity in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When firing upon enemy targets, did your brigade heavy weapons utilise direct or indirect mode of fire?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: In my previous answer, I said that when we selected the positions of deployment of our artillery group, we made sure that they are deployed in such a place where they could open direct fire on the enemy. This is how we ensured better precision, much better than if we were to open indirect mode of fire through our officers on the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I would like to move to so-called modified aerial bombs. First, can you tell us your knowledge of what these bombs were?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: First of all, I could say that the name itself, a modified aerial bomb, is not adequate. It is not adequate because we never made any modifications on the air bomb. Fuel contact bombs that we used were the kind of bombs that were once used by the JNA airforce. The only thing that we changed was the mode of use; i.e., the mode of launching such bombs. Based on my experience, I can tell you that it was made much more precise in that way than if it was used from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what steps your brigade undertook to minimise the deviations in the aerial bombs when launched?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I can say that my brigade, once it received launchers and the appropriate components to manufacturer such bombs, not aerial bombs but just the modifications, as you call them, the first thing we did was to choose an adequate position. The positions that we chose also allowed us to have optical visibility with the target. The second thing that we bore in mind was for such bombs to be launched in favorable weather conditions, when it was not foggy, when it was not very windy, in order to increase the precision of those bombs. You have to know that such bombs were launched over our own heads. Any - even marginal - errors could have cost us dearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just have a clarification question. Sir, you said at page 79, line 14: "Based on my experience, I can tell you that it was made much more precise in that way than if it was used from the air." Can you explain to us how it operates when it's from the air and how it operates from the way you used it and show us why it is more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I can explain. When a pilot launches an aerial bomb, the precision of those classical bombs without any guidance system is contingent upon the capability of such a pilot to do a timely launch. In practice, it happened that it took several attempts to hit the target that was selected. On the other hand, we had launchers and we had optical visibility with the target. We could measure the distance very precisely, and that's how we achieved a higher level of precision. I am speaking from experience. I launched three aerial bombs myself; i.e., my brigade did. So what I'm telling you is based on that experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, were there firing tables for the aerial bomb launcher?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Of course. We received launchers and firing tables which were temporary firing tables for aerial bombs. On those firing tables, you could see the angles and the distances, so the crew could put in precise distances into their device. Everything else would have been improvisation. Those temporary firing tables were glued to the launcher very visible to the eye of the crew, and we did not have any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ascertain if the launchers for the modified aerial bombs had been tested?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Of course. Not a single piece of armament or weaponry that is introduced into a military is introduced without previously being tested by the manufacturer. In this specific case, as far as I know, that testing was done at Kalinovik, which is an old artillery shooting range intended for such testings. And the firing tables we received were based and crafted based upon those testings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the three modified aerial bombs that you said your brigade launched, could you give us some more details about the targets they were launched at and your appraisals of their accuracy.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: When we were equipped with the aerial bomb launcher, before we launched our first bomb on the enemy, I wanted to test its efficiency and precision. That's why I issued an order that the first target for us would be the cooler plant near Stup. Let me explain. This is a concrete -- reinforced concrete facility. It was 70 by 70 metres large, and its height was about 70 metres as well. Throughout the entire war, that facility was a place from which sniper fire was opened at us by the enemy. In order to complete the first launch, I moved our soldiers from the first line to the left and to the right, and we had a direct hit of the cooler plant. We didn't want the first bomb to overfly the cooler plant. That's why I asked the crew of the launcher to decrease the elevation so that we made sure that it wouldn't overfly. When we launched that aerial bomb, because the elevation was short, it was not adequate, the bomb actually did not hit the target itself. It fell short, some hundred metres in front of the target. It fell at -- on its side and it slid like a bobsleigh. That was our first launch. It was not successful, but it didn't make me unhappy because I could see how it acted. The second bomb was launched on the 28th July, 1995 on the television building of Sarajevo. Throughout the war, it was the television of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army. The darkest kind of propaganda was launched from there against my people. When I received -- when I received approval from my superior command, I personally assisted the launch of that aerial bomb. I was at the observation post, and I saw that the aerial bomb hit the building of the radio television, and that made me very happy. The third aerial bomb was launched on the Aleksa Santic school in Hrasnica. It was school only by name. However, throughout the war it housed the centre for the training of special units of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army. How did I know that? On Muslim television, their president, Alija Izetbegovic, was shown visiting the 104th Brigade of the BiH Army, and he also visited that school, and he commended them for successfully completed education. Having heard that, when I received my orders from the superior command, I launched the third aerial bomb, and that was the only target that we missed but by only 20 metres. Let me explain. When an aerial bomb hits the ground, since it is a contact fuse shell; i.e., it is not intended for targeting troops or targets in the open space. It is intended for hitting facilities. The crater that it made was 5 metres deep and its diameter was 15 metres, which only goes to show that most of the kinetic energy of that aerial bomb was used for its dispersion. So this is the long and short of the story of the aerial bombs that we launched during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one more question on the aerial bombs before moving on. The first one bomb -- the first bomb launched at the cooler plant, did it explode when it skid like a bobsled?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: No, it did not explode. It remained there. Even I -- after the Dayton Accords were signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you done with this subject, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a question on that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a clarification to avoid any misunderstanding. I see on the transcript that you said; that is, page 82, lines 11 and 12: "Throughout the war, the television building was the television of the 1st Corps of the BH Army." Was that really what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is what I meant to say. 90 per cent of their programme was pure propaganda. We were portrayed as the biggest criminals. I believe that then and I still believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This was not my question. I wanted to know if the 1st Corps of the BH Army had its own television.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, their television was Television Sarajevo; i.e., the television of Bosnia Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was the reason why I put this question to you, because you are recorded as having said: "Throughout the war, this building was the television of the 1st Corps of the BH Army."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to highlight what they did because they used that television as their own. That was what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also have one or more questions for you. You said there were firing tables for the air bombs but they were temporary. Could you explain what makes a firing table a temporary one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't receive translation at this moment, but...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since there was a temporary table of firing, there must have been a permanent one too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is -- well, that's not necessary. If you have a temporary one, there can just be a temporary one. There -- you do not receive -- yes. Now how -- from whom did you get a temporary timetable -- timetable. Firing table? Who did -- who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received it from the corps command, and they, in turn, had received it from the manufacturer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Manufacturer of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The manufacturer of launchers and the manufacturer of the engines mounted on the air bombs. They also carried out the testing of those bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any test reports then? Because we have received some evidence about how the engines were mounted on the air bombs, and we have not received that much evidence on the production of launchers. But could you tell us a bit more in detail what these test reports, what they contained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rocket launchers were manufactured by us based on the sketches we received from our superior command. The basis -- or the base was actually a truck with a back that could be lifted up and down. We used it to mount launchers on top of it. A bomb would be fitted onto a launcher, and with much electronics, an air bomb would be launched provided a proper angle was chosen in order to reach a certain distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand what you need to come to some precision. But what I asked you is whether there were testing reports. Because at least there are three parties involved; that is, the producer of the launcher, the producer of the engines, then I take it the production of the modified air bomb in such a way that the engines were attached to the bomb itself. And then, as a fourth element, how the launchers were mounted on -- on trucks. That requires a rather complex system where testing is not that easily done. Could you tell us were there testing reports? Test reports, I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The engines used to launch air bombs had been tested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they had undergone many years of testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I interrupt you quite direct. What I meant to ask you is whether this system, not the specific elements, but whether the system was tested, because I noticed that there are various components which, when putting them together, would perhaps give a totally different result. If you attach an engine 1 centimetre further to the left or to the right, that might have had a huge impact on the precision of the system as such. So, therefore, I'm wondering - and I'm asking you - whether there were any test reports on the system as functioning composed of these elements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not carry out testing. We received bombs already fitted with the engines and that had been done in the Pretis factory in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you how you received them. I'm asking whether there were test reports about the system as such.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. But they were not available to me. I was a brigade commander. I didn't need such data. I needed firing tables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say they were there but they were not available to you. How do you know that they did exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there would have been no firing tables without testing. No weapon is introduced in to -- or put into use without previous testing. Everything else would be fooling around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's logic rather than factual knowledge you are giving us. Now back to the temporary -- the temporary tables, firing tables. You say if there are firing tables, there must be test reports. What made them temporary? I mean, why after proper testing and the standardised production procedure? You would just produce the firing tables, I would say, rather than temporary firing tables. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly can. The entire arsenal of our units - and I mean the artillery and mortars - we had standing firing tables, which were published as manuals, and I had occasion to see one such manual here; thus, they are available to you. For this kind of assets which, to an extent, was improvised, there were no standing firing tables, only provisional ones. It was not something that was part of the JNA arsenal. That asset was produced for one particular use, and our experts relied on air bombs, and with certain additions, they managed to create a very successful asset that we used to defend ourselves. That is why those firing tables were provisional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what I hear you say is that you have no detailed knowledge about the testing, the procedure; you have no detailed knowledge about the production because it was all fitted already, and how it was fitted, at least, you haven't told us; and that you received firing tables which were more or less improvised. Now this ends up in saying that the position was deviation not more than 10 metres or 10 metres on 1 kilometre trajectory. Where do you get that from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I have to say that we didn't improvise. What I said was that the provisional firing tables were put together after a process of testing. So it wasn't all improvisation. That's number one. Number two, I also stated that it was the experience of our brigade that we were very precise and that there was no deviation larger than 10 metres per 1 kilometre. I don't know about the experience of other units, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us about three launches. One failure, but there at least you -- you know how it worked. And then the two others. Is your assessment of the accuracy, is that based on those two other launches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's on the basis of these. And you didn't include the third one which failed to hit the target. Did you include something like what the Chamber heard evidence about, a launch of such a modified air bomb to be a total failure even killing people from your own armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't aware of any such information during the war. I can only discuss my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you -- no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- bomb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know, the answer is you can't tell us. May I remind you that when I -- let me see -- yes. You said that when I put to you the question about matters being improvised, you said, well, you didn't say that. May I read to you what is recorded as what you would have said: "For these kind of assets which, to an extent, was improvised, there were no standard firing tables." So when I used the word "improvised," I just repeated your own words. Unless there is any mistake in translation. I leave it to that at this moment. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Moloto also has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, let me just make sure that I understood you clearly. When you described the precision -- are we together, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. When you describe the precision of your modified aerial bombs, you said that you used laser and therefore they are very precise, margin of error 1 centimetre short because the 1 centimetre, well, you clarified that it was measuring a deviation in distance. And when you talked about targeting the three other targets that you launched, you said one of your bombs fell short by 20 metres. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the first target we targeted was missed. Due to low elevation, the bomb undershot and went unexploded. The second target was the TV building; that was hit. The third target was the school building, and the bomb overshot, falling into a meadow 20 metres further away, creating a crater 5 metres deep and 15 metres wide. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I obviously misunderstood you. I thought you said it fell short. So it overshot by 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So instead of measuring -- getting a deviation of 1 centimetre, as you had indicated, it had a deviation of 20 metres. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't understand me correctly. I said that the precision of the laser distance measurement is measured in centimetres and that is one initial element of firing in order to obtain the precise distance of the target. If the laser measurement indicates that it is, say, 250 metres away, the potential margin of error is a few centimetres. But it doesn't mean that the air bomb would behave the same as the laser measurement device because its trajectory is governed by different principles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought when you were explaining -- when you explain that deviation of a centimetres, you were explaining how precise the modified air bomb is better than the one that is carried by a plane. You told us that the one that is carried by the plane, it depends on the capability of the pilot to see exactly where that target is. But this one was guided by -- it was modified such that it hits the target as you measured it with a laser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to see whether we can come to a proper understanding of your words, because they created apparently some confusion. Would it be true that the measurement of distances with your laser gauge was separate from any firing system but was just used to measure a distance, whereas the variation there would -- or the deviation would be very limited. Whereas when firing projectiles, that you were facing far more and other circumstances which would allow for deviations which are -- were far in excess of the deviations you would have if you would only measure a distance. Is that...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I wanted to say. A laser range finder determines the distance, but it is only an initial element of firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll be with us for more time, so we'll have ample opportunity to further explore what exactly you intended to say. You see, ballistics are always the core of the interest of this Chamber because it's an important matter. Mr. Ivetic, when I encouraged you to finish by 2.00 then, of course, it was not included that we had so many questions. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have approximately seven questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seven questions, yes. Well, that should be approximately 10 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to 15 minutes. Okay. Witness, we'll adjourn for the day. We would like to see you back tomorrow at 9.30 and -- one second, please. One second. Witness. Yes, I'd like to give you further instructions. That is, that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given today or whether that is testimony which you are still about to give tomorrow and perhaps the day or days after that. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 26th of June at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
